content: 1. If a live-virus vaccine is administered within 28 days (4 weeks) of another live-virus vaccine, there is a potential for interference in the immune response. 2. A study conducted in two U.S. health maintenance organizations found that the risk of varicella vaccine failure (varicella disease in a vaccinated person) was three times higher among individuals who received the varicella vaccine within 28 days of an MMR vaccination compared to those who received it more than 28 days after the MMR vaccination. 3. Another study determined that the immune response to the yellow fever vaccine is not affected by a monovalent measles vaccine administered 1–27 days earlier. 4. The effect of non-simultaneous administration of rubella, mumps, varicella, and yellow fever vaccines is unknown. 5. To minimize the potential risk of interference, injectable or nasally administered live vaccines not given on the same day should be administered at least 4 weeks apart. 6. If injectable or nasally administered live vaccines are separated by less than 4 weeks, the last dose is considered invalid and should be repeated. 7. Oral vaccines, such as Ty21a typhoid and rotavirus vaccines, can be administered simultaneously or at any interval before or after other live vaccines (injectable or intranasal) if indicated. 8. Live vaccines, such as Ty21a typhoid, yellow fever, LAIV, zoster, and rotavirus vaccines, may be administered at any time before, concurrently with, or after administration of immune globulin, hyperimmune globulin, or intravenous immune globulin (IGIV). 9. Blood products (e.g., whole blood, packed red blood cells, plasma) and other antibody-containing blood products (e.g., immune globulin, hyperimmune globulin, and IGIV) can inhibit the immune response to measles and rubella vaccines for more than 3 months. 10. The effect of blood and immune globulin preparations on the response to mumps and varicella vaccines is unknown; however, commercial immune globulin preparations contain antibodies to these viruses. 11. Blood products available in the United States are unlikely to contain substantial amounts of antibody to the yellow fever vaccine virus. 12. The duration of interference with injectable live-virus vaccines (other than yellow fever) after administration of an antibody-containing product depends on the amount of antigen-specific antibody in the product. 13. After receiving an antibody-containing product, live vaccines (other than yellow fever, oral Ty21a typhoid, LAIV, zoster, and rotavirus) should be delayed until the passive antibody has degraded. 14. If a dose of injectable live-virus vaccine (other than yellow fever and zoster) is administered after an antibody-containing product but at an interval shorter than recommended, the vaccine dose should be repeated unless serologic testing indicates a response to the vaccine. 15. The repeat dose or serologic testing should be performed after the interval indicated for the antibody-containing product. 16. Passively acquired antibodies can interfere with the response to rubella vaccine, but the low dose of anti-Rho(D) globulin administered to postpartum women has not been shown to reduce the response to the RA27/3 strain rubella vaccine. 17. Because of the importance of rubella and varicella immunity among women of childbearing age, postpartum vaccination of women without evidence of immunity to rubella or varicella with MMR, varicella, or MMRV vaccines should not be delayed because of receipt of anti-Rho(D) globulin or any other blood product during the last trimester of pregnancy or at delivery. 18. 19. Interference might occur if administration of an antibody-containing product becomes necessary after administration of MMR or varicella vaccines. 20. Usually, vaccine virus replication and stimulation of immunity occur 1–2 weeks after vaccination. 21. If the interval between administration of any of these vaccines and subsequent administration of an antibody-containing product is less than 14 days, vaccination should be repeated after the recommended interval unless serologic testing indicates a protective antibody response. 22. A humanized mouse monoclonal antibody product (palivizumab) is available as prophylaxis for serious lower respiratory tract disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus among infants and young children. 23. This product contains only antibody to respiratory syncytial virus and does not interfere with the immune response to licensed live or inactivated vaccines. 24. Antibody-containing products interact less with inactivated vaccines, toxoids, recombinant subunit, and polysaccharide vaccines than with live vaccines. 25. Administering inactivated vaccines and toxoids either simultaneously with or at any interval before or after receipt of an antibody-containing product should not substantially impair the development of a protective antibody response. 26. The vaccine or toxoid and antibody preparation should be administered at different sites using the standard recommended dose. 27. Increasing the vaccine dose volume or number of vaccinations is not indicated or recommended. 28. Certain vaccines that provide protection from the same diseases are available from different manufacturers, and these vaccines are usually not identical in antigen content or in the amount or method of formulation. 29. Manufacturers use different production processes, and their products might contain different concentrations of antigen per dose or a different stabilizer or preservative. 30. Available data indicate that infants who receive sequential doses of different Hib conjugate, hepatitis B, and hepatitis A vaccines produce a satisfactory antibody response after a complete primary series. 31. All brands of Hib conjugate, hepatitis B, hepatitis A, rotavirus, and quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccines are interchangeable within their respective series. 32. If different brands of a particular vaccine require a different number of doses for series completion (e.g., Hib and rotavirus vaccines) and a provider mixes brands, the higher number of doses is recommended for series completion. 33. Limited data are available about the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of using acellular pertussis (e.g., DTaP) vaccines from different manufacturers for successive doses of the pertussis series. 34. 35. However, in the absence of a clear serologic correlate of protection for pertussis, the relevance of these immunogenicity data for protection against pertussis is unknown. 36. When feasible, the same brand of DTaP vaccine should be used for all doses of the vaccination series.
